questions.stem: Article 131 of the Indian Constitution grants the Supreme Court 'Original Jurisdiction'. Which of the following disputes falls EXCLUSIVELY under the Original Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court?

options.option_text: A dispute between the Government of India and one or more States
A dispute regarding the election of a Member of Parliament
A dispute between two private citizens regarding a fundamental rights violation
A dispute regarding the sharing of inter-state river waters

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: 'Original Jurisdiction' means the power of a court to hear a case for the very FIRST time, rather than on appeal. Under Article 131, the Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction over disputes of a federal nature: i.e., Centre vs State, or State vs State. No other court in India can hear these cases.
DECOY BUSTING: 
- MP election disputes go to the High Court first.
- Fundamental rights violations (Art 32) are Original, but NOT EXCLUSIVE (because you can also go to the High Court under Art 226).
- Inter-state water disputes (Art 262) are explicitly EXCLUDED from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction by law; they go to specialized Water Tribunals.
EXAM INSIGHT: If a private citizen sues the Centre, it does not fall under Article 131. It must strictly be a dispute between the constituent units of the Indian federation.
questions.subject: Polity

questions.stem: Under which Article can the President of India seek the 'Advisory Opinion' of the Supreme Court on any question of law or fact of public importance?

options.option_text: Article 143
Article 137
Article 129
Article 132

questions.explanation:
WHY IT IS CORRECT: Under Article 143, the President can refer any matter of public importance to the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion. (For example, the Presidential reference on the 2G spectrum allocation or the Ayodhya dispute). 
DECOY BUSTING: 
- Article 137 is the Review Jurisdiction (the SC can review its own past judgments).
- Article 129 makes the SC a 'Court of Record' (its judgments are precedents, and it can punish for contempt).
- Article 132 deals with Appellate Jurisdiction in constitutional cases.
EXAM INSIGHT: Crucially, the Supreme Court is NOT bound to give its opinion on every reference (it refused to give an opinion on the Ayodhya reference). Furthermore, if the SC does give an opinion, the President is NOT legally bound to accept it. It is purely advisory.

questions.stem: Which Article of the Constitution empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, making it their direct guardian?

options.option_text: Article 13, which voids laws violating Fundamental Rights
Article 32, which grants the right to approach SC directly
Article 226, which is the High Court's writ-issuing power
Article 21, which protects life and personal liberty broadly

questions.explanation: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right that empowers citizens to move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights; the SC can issue writs (habeas corpus, mandamus, etc.) under it. Article 226 is the analogous power of High Courts but is NOT a Fundamental Right. Article 13 only declares violative laws void — it does not confer writ jurisdiction.

questions.stem: Under Article 141 of the Indian Constitution, the law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on which of the following?

options.option_text: Only the High Courts within their respective territorial jurisdictions
All courts and tribunals throughout the territory of India
Only courts that are directly subordinate to the High Courts
All courts except statutory tribunals and quasi-judicial forums

questions.explanation: Article 141 uses the phrase 'all courts within the territory of India,' and the Supreme Court has further held that this extends to tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies as well. Option A is wrong because Article 141 binds every court, including High Courts themselves, not just those below them. Option D is wrong because tribunals are equally bound per judicial interpretation.

questions.stem: Article 136(2) of the Constitution explicitly bars the Supreme Court from granting Special Leave to Appeal against orders passed by which category of courts or tribunals?

options.option_text: Courts exercising civil jurisdiction in matters involving Union of India
Statutory tribunals set up under central legislation such as NCLT and NGT
Courts or tribunals constituted under laws relating to the Armed Forces
High Courts exercising original jurisdiction in commercial matters

questions.explanation: Article 136(2) expressly excludes any 'judgment, determination, sentence or order passed or made by any court or tribunal constituted by or under any law relating to the Armed Forces.' This is the only explicit constitutional bar on SLP. Many candidates confuse this with NCLT or NGT orders, which can still be challenged via SLP before the Supreme Court.

questions.stem: The Supreme Court's power under Article 142 to do 'complete justice' is exercisable in the exercise of which of its jurisdictions?

options.option_text: Only its original jurisdiction in inter-state disputes under Article 131
Only its appellate jurisdiction under Articles 132, 133, and 134
Any cause or matter pending before it across all its jurisdictions
Only in writ petitions filed directly under Article 32 of the Constitution

questions.explanation: Article 142(1) reads 'in the exercise of its jurisdiction' — an unrestricted phrase that covers all jurisdictions: original, appellate, advisory, and writ. The Supreme Court has used Article 142 in SLP matters, contempt proceedings, and even suo motu cases. Confining it to Article 131 or Article 32 alone is a common error because those are the most litigated contexts where Article 142 visibly operates.

questions.stem: Under Article 137, the Supreme Court may review its own judgments. Which of the following is a recognised ground for filing a Review Petition before the Supreme Court?

options.option_text: When the petitioner believes the court's legal reasoning was erroneous
An error apparent on the face of the record or discovery of new evidence
When a subsequent larger bench of the Supreme Court takes a contrary position
When the judgment conflicts with a provision of any central legislation

questions.explanation: The Supreme Court's Rules limit review to: (i) discovery of new and important evidence not available earlier, (ii) an error apparent on the face of the record, or (iii) any other sufficient reason of a like nature. Mere disagreement with legal reasoning is NOT a ground — that would convert Review into a disguised appeal. A contrary decision by a larger bench would be addressed via a reference or curative petition, not a review.

questions.stem: Under Article 139A(1), if the same substantial question of law is pending before both the Supreme Court and one or more High Courts, which action may the Supreme Court take?

options.option_text: Transfer all such cases to a single High Court for a consolidated hearing
Issue an advisory opinion to the High Courts resolving the legal question
Withdraw the cases from the High Courts and dispose of all of them itself
Stay all High Court proceedings until a Constitution Bench resolves the question

questions.explanation: Article 139A(1) specifically empowers the Supreme Court to 'withdraw the case or cases pending before the High Court or the High Courts and dispose of all the cases itself' when the same substantial question of law of general importance is involved. Option A is wrong because transfer to a High Court is the power under Article 139A(2) when similar cases are pending between two High Courts, not this sub-clause. Option B (advisory opinion) is the Article 143 power and requires a Presidential reference.

questions.stem: In Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), the Supreme Court evolved the 'Curative Petition'. Which of the following was held as a mandatory procedural condition for its admission?

options.option_text: It must be filed within 30 days of the dismissal of the Review Petition
It must cite a later Supreme Court judgment that directly reverses the ruling
It must allege violation of natural justice and carry a Senior Advocate's certificate
It must be placed before a bench of at least seven judges of the Supreme Court

questions.explanation: In Rupa Hurra, the court laid down that a Curative Petition must (i) allege either that a party was not heard (violation of natural justice) or that a judge on the bench was biased, AND (ii) be certified by a Senior Advocate on record as meeting those grounds. There is no fixed 30-day limitation (Option A). Option D is wrong — the petition is circulated to the three senior-most judges and the judge(s) who passed the order; if a majority agrees, it is heard by the same bench, not a 7-judge bench.
